kernelIdea: If the first domino falls, and every domino knocks over the next, then all of them fall. Pattern-spotting suggests a claim; induction turns the guess into knowledge.

kernels.l1: Push the first one, and make sure each one can reach the next. Then they all fall.
kernels.l2: A row of dominoes all falls if two things are true: somebody pushes the first, and each one is close enough to knock over the next. Miss either and the row stops.
kernels.l3: If a claim is true for the first case, and being true for one case always makes it true for the next, then it is true for every case. Spotting a pattern is a guess; the domino argument is what turns the guess into knowledge.
kernels.l4: Dominoes: if the first falls and each one knocks over the next, all fall. Applied to statements, this is induction — and it is needed because a pattern holding for many cases is not evidence that it holds for all.
kernels.l5: Induction is the domino principle for statements indexed by integers; pattern-spotting generates conjectures but cannot establish them, as counterexamples appearing only at n = 40 demonstrate.
kernels.l6: The two domino conditions correspond exactly to the base case and the inductive step; either failing breaks the chain.
kernels.l7: The domino picture — first falls, each knocks the next — is the intuition behind induction. Pattern-spotting suggests; only the two conditions establish, since a pattern can persist for arbitrarily many cases and then fail.
kernels.l8: Induction is equivalent to well-ordering of ℕ and is Peano’s ninth axiom; the domino picture is a faithful rendering of that axiom.
